The triangular geometry coherently distributes energy into two quantum batteries, where mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization gives rise to collective energy storage.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Symmetry governs the organization of physical structures, while symmetry breaking reveals their transformations. In geometric deep learning, symmetry imposes rank constraints on equivariant representations, limiting the expressive capacity of equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs). Here we show that these constraints can instead be exploited: the singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide a unified fingerprint of structural symmetry. We introduce spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which enable discrete point-group identification through rank-template matching and continuous symmetry analysis by quantifying spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enabling a parameter-free GNN implementation. Its spectra can be reused across multiple target groups, and the resulting leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, SymFP accurately identifies point groups, tracks controlled symmetry breaking and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that can be obscured by global geometric measures. These results establish the spectral structure of equivariant representations as a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Autotaxis of a Run-and-Tumble Agent via Reinforcement Learning
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We study the run-tumble motion of a single autochemotactic agent that secretes and senses chemical cues using a reinforcement learning (RL) framework. In a chemical environment that changes dynamically via secretion, diffusion, and degradation of attractant chemicals, we study the effectiveness of RL for a successful navigation strategy. We show that RL enhances chemotactic performance. Starting from a random initial position, the probability of finding the agent in the favorable region (near the attractant peak) increases faster with time and reaches a higher value in the long time limit when RL is used, compared to the case when the agent performs usual run-tumble chemotaxis without using RL. We also characterize the chemotactic performance of the agent by varying different parameters like rates of secretion, degradation, and diffusion. Importantly, we observe a non-monotonic dependence of the chemotactic performance on the learning and exploration rates, indicating the existence of an optimal RL strategy for the most efficient navigation. We explain these observations as a result of the interplay between the pre-existing attractant environment and the agent-generated attractant profile.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Exact and Near-Exact Inverse Renormalization Group with Constrained Monte Carlo
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We establish conditions for exactness of the inverse renormalization group via constrained Markov processes, a class of Monte Carlo simulations which sample the degrees of freedom within a block on a fine lattice under the constraint that they remain consistent with the corresponding degree of freedom on the coarse lattice according to a forward renormalization group transformation. We show analytically, for an arbitrary transformation, that constrained Markov processes correspond to an exact inversion of the renormalization group at the fixed point action, and to a near-exact inversion in the vicinity of the fixed point. We then optimize renormalization group transformations directly on inversely renormalized configurations to effectively map the action onto itself and ensure computational stability in the generation of configurations for high-dimensional systems. Starting from a set of uncorrelated configurations for the three-dimensional $\phi^{4}$ quantum field theory at lattice volume $V=16^{3}$, we invert the renormalization group with constrained Monte Carlo to construct a set of uncorrelated, near-equilibrium configurations for $V=128^{3}$ and extract two critical exponents of the system. The inversion exhibits no critical slowing down, with dynamic critical exponent $z=0.03(2)$.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection
arXiv_CondMat.summary: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Continuum Photonic Axion Insulators
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Here, I study the conditions for realizing an axion topology in a homogeneous inversion-symmetric electromagnetic continuum, in the absence of a crystalline lattice. I introduce a continuum inversion invariant expressed solely in terms of the spectral properties of the material response in the zero- and infinite-wave-vector limits. Surprisingly, it is found that standard gyrotropic-type material responses are strongly constrained and, under fairly general conditions, cannot open an axion gap within first-order perturbation theory. Based on an analogy between the effective response of crystalline photonic axion insulators and the optical response of centrosymmetric altermagnets, a class of spatially dispersive odd magnetoelectric couplings that can open an axion gap is identified. These findings suggest an interesting hierarchy of nonreciprocal mechanisms in electromagnetic continua: while uniform gyrotropy relates to Chern phases, odd magnetoelectric coupling relates to axion phases.

arXiv_CondMat.title: A Passive Intelligent Metasurface: A Network Model
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Intelligent metasurfaces enable advanced wave manipulation, including negative refraction, focusing, beam splitting and beam steering, with significant potential for practical applications. However, conventional approaches often rely on active metamaterials with gain, or demand computationally intensive solutions of inverse problems to find the optimal configuration. In this work, we use the scattering framework of quantum graph theory to derive an exact, analytic expression for configuration of a passive metasurface that produces a prescribed reflected wave field. The metasurface terminates a periodic lattice of waveguides and consists of an array of channels, each a tube of length $\ell_m$ ending in a vertex whose scattering parameter $\lambda_m$ sets how much of the wave is lost to the wall. For any prescribed incident and reflected field, the exact lengths and scattering parameters follow channel by channel, in closed form, from the ratio of the wave amplitudes returning to and leaving the lattice, and the metasurface is passive whenever this ratio does not exceed unity in modulus. We demonstrate the construction for both a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional metasurface. The one-dimensional metasurface terminates a two-dimensional lattice and steers, splits or perfectly absorbs Gaussian beams. The two-dimensional metasurface terminates a three-dimensional lattice and generates a prescribed image in a plane inside the lattice. In each case, we obtain the exact boundary properties that produce the effect.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Monopoles, Scattering and Generalized Symmetries on a Quantum Computer
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Quantum computers have advanced to the stage that interesting many-body quantum phenomena can be observed. A striking example is the magnetic monopole paradox, a problem that was only solved recently using the language of generalized symmetries. Here we demonstrate a quantum spin chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on Quantinuum System Model H2. We implement a novel protocol for preparing a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. By combining this protocol with time evolution across a duality defect, we efficiently convert local particles into non-local string-like excitations. We demonstrate this particle-to-string conversion in the transverse-field Ising model and a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase of the cluster model. Our results establish duality defects and generalized symmetries as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Quantifying the remaining search space in analogue optimisation
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Benchmarking analogue optimisers requires certifying not only how close a returned energy is to the optimum, but also how many better configurations may remain. Semidefinite relaxations provide rigorous bounds on the ground-state energy and selected observables, yet reveal little about the size of this residual search space. We introduce a deterministic, instance-specific upper bound on the number of binary configurations whose energies improve upon a returned state by a prescribed margin. Combined with a semidefinite energy interval, this yields a complementary certificate of both the magnitude and multiplicity of any possible improvement. To judge an analogue optimiser's native performance, we provide a generalisation of the framework to obtain bounds on the Haar volume of the remaining continuous phase-space. To further characterise the remaining search space, we extend our bounds to resolve regions in configuration space in both the binary and continuous setting. Our approach couples a variational-Chernoff reduction with an elimination bound of the resulting partition function. Comparisons with exact enumeration and independent Haar sampling are consistent with the bounds on small instances. In numerical experiments at $N=1000$, even the largest family-median bound restricts the potentially improving binary configurations to less than $10^{-144}$ of the full configuration space, while the largest upper bound on the corresponding Haar volume is of order $10^{-499}$.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
arXiv_CondMat.summary: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Coupling between molecular exchange qubits
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Spin triangles are promising systems for defining and manipulating scalar degrees of freedom, such as chirality, partial spin sums, or combinations between the two. Here we extend this analysis to dimers formed by pairs of spin triangles, coupled by exchange or dipolar interactions. We show that the weak-coupling limit warrants the introduction of an effective two-qubit picture, and derive the expressions of the related Hamiltonians as a function of the underlying physical interaction between the triangles. We benchmark this two-qubit Hamiltonian against the microscopic one, and discuss the observable effects of the inter-triangle coupling on the spin-electric transitions between states with different chiralities or partial-spin sums.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Accessing Fractional Wilson Lines from U(1) Monodromy Defects on the Fuzzy Sphere
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Wilson lines are gauge-invariant probes of charge screening and deconfinement, which can detect the response of quantum critical matter to an external charge, but their universal information at strongly-coupled critical points remains hard to access. Here we investigate a continuous family of $U(1)$ monodromy defects of the three-dimensional $O(2)$ Wilson--Fisher conformal field theory, which is dual to fractional Wilson lines in the critical noncompact Abelian Higgs model with one unit-charged scalar. We realize this continuous family of defects within the fuzzy-sphere framework by threading a fractional Aharonov--Bohm flux through the two poles of the sphere. We observe the emergence of charged operators carrying fractional transverse spins, as a characteristic signature of the imposed monodromy. The appearance of displacement operator at its protected dimension supports the conformal nature of this defect line. Crucially, we resolve no relevant symmetry-preserving defect scalar, and identify charge-one monopole operators as relevant symmetry-breaking deformations. Assuming the duality, these results provide non-perturbative evidence that fractional Wilson lines of the critical Abelian Higgs model are stable conformal lines.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Dualities in one-dimensional quantum lattice models: Lie groups, Schur-Weyl duality and symmetry breaking
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We present a systematic framework for gauging continuous symmetries, and show that the Schur-Weyl duality arises naturally as a realization of this construction with open boundary conditions. Restricting to compact Lie group symmetries, we construct dual models for one-dimensional quantum lattice models exhibiting those symmetries. We demonstrate that matrix product operators enable the explicit construction of intertwiners between the dual theories and their (non-invertible) symmetries. With closed boundary conditions, we can relate the full spectrum of these dual theories by considering all possible twisted boundary conditions.We illustrate how the Peter-Weyl transform appears when the duality acts on the boundary Hilbert space of a $G$-symmetric model. The presented framework generalizes previous work on dualities for unitary fusion category symmetric models. It exemplifies how dualities for both finite and continuous symmetries rely on the relation between a bond algebra and a representation of the symmetry in the lattice as double centralizers. We argue that dual non-invertible spontaneous symmetry breaking is the mechanism that underlies symmetric tensor network algorithms. We illustrate these results for $U(1)$- and $SU(2)$-symmetric quantum lattice models.

arXiv_CondMat.title: A Simple Approach to the Complexity of Mean Field Ising Spin Glasses
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The geometry of spherical spin glasses is relatively well understood, thanks in large part to the Kac-Rice formula. However, this formula does not directly apply to discrete spin systems, and much less is known mathematically about the geometry of Ising spin glasses. In this paper, we present a simple method for counting local optima and gapped states in a broad class of discrete spin glasses. To illustrate its scope, we compute the annealed complexities ("configurational entropies," in the physics language) of mixed Ising spin glasses with potentials, such as external fields, and of the Ghatak-Sherrington model. These computations recover several existing results in the mathematics and physics literature as special cases. We can also compute energy-constrained complexity, finding a critical energy threshold analogous to the spherical case, but for gapped states of pure Ising spin glasses. Finally, we use our method to establish a form of disorder persistence for gapped states, identifying a transition between $3$-spin and $4$-spin glasses.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as $L^{-1/2}$ with chain length $L$ only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Defect Anomalies at a Distance
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Surface defects carry Weyl and gravitational anomalies that generalize the central charges of two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) and characterize the anomalous response of gapless surface modes to background geometry. These anomalies usually appear as contact terms on the defect. We explain how they are encoded at a distance, in scheme-independent integrated bulk stress-tensor correlators. We derive sum rules for them in terms of defect operator data, establish a lower bound on the boundary Weyl anomaly in three-dimensional CFTs, and illustrate our results with explicit examples.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Magnetism modulation in Co3Sn2S2 by current-assisted domain wall motion
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The efficiency of spintronic devices can be improved by generating higher effective magnetic fields with lower working currents. Spin-transfer torques can drive magnetic domain wall motion in a device composed of a single material, but a high threshold current density is typically required to move the domain wall and improving the effective magnetic field in common itinerant ferromagnets is difficult. Here we report magnetism modulation in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$, a magnetic Weyl semimetal, via spin-transfer-torque-driven domain wall motion. We examine the effect of d.c. current on magnetic reversal using anomalous Hall resistance measurements and domain wall motion using time-of-flight measurements. At 160 K, the threshold current density for driving domain wall motion is less than $5.1\times10^5$ A cm$^{-2}$ at zero external field and less than $1.5\times10^5$ A cm$^{-2}$ at a moderate external field (0.2 kOe). The spin-transfer-torque effective field can reach as high as 2.4 to 5.6 kOe MA$^{-1}$ cm$^2$ at 150 K.

arXiv_CondMat.title: A General Solution for Network Models with Pairwise Edge Coupling
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Network Models with couplings between link pairs are the simplest models for a class of networks with Higher Order interactions. In this paper we give an analytic, general solution to this family of Random Graph Models extending previous results obtained for specific interaction structures. We use the Hubbard-Stratonovich transform to show that such higher order models can be decoupled into families of effectively separable random graph models, which might be enhanced with auxiliary, possibly multi-valued, parameters identifying the thermodynamical phase of the system. Moreover, given the diagonalizability of couplings between links, we carry out the full computation of the partition functions and discuss why in some cases they can effectively reduce to the one for the Mean-Field case.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Evolution from intralayer to interlayer superconductivity in a bilayer $t$-$J$-$J_{\bot}$ ladder
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Motivated by the bilayer cuprate superconductors and nickelate superconductor La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, we investigate the evolution from intralayer to interlayer superconductivity in finite-width bilayer $t$-$J$-$J_{\bot}$ ladders, where $t$ is the in-plane electron hopping, $J$ is the in-plane spin interaction, and $J_{\bot}$ is the inter-plane spin interaction. By means of the density matrix renormalization group calculations, we map out the quantum phase diagram of the bilayer two-leg ladders by tuning $J_{\bot}$ in a large doping range $\delta = 1/8 - 1/2$. We find that a large $J_{\bot}$ can always drive an interlayer superconductivity by coupling the two layers in both the Luther-Emery liquid and Luttinger liquid states. By coupling two Luther-Emery liquid states, the in-plane superconductivity evolves to inter-plane superconductivity either through an intermediate charge density wave (CDW) phase or directly, depending on doping ratio. This emergent CDW phase, which exists over a finite doping range, appears to develop from the CDW state of the two-leg ladder at $\delta = 1/4$. By coupling two Luttinger liquids, the in-plane Luttinger liquids show a transition to the inter-plane superconducting phase at large $J_{\bot}$, as reported in previous literature. Interestingly, in the intermediate $J_{\bot}$ regime we find that while the in-plane Luttinger-liquid features remain stable, the inter-plane superconductivity can develop an enhanced quasi-long-range order with the power exponent $K^{zz}_{\rm SC} \sim 1$. At last, we show that the interlayer superconductivity is also stable by coupling the bilayer three-leg $t$-$J$ ladders by a strong $J_{\bot}$ interaction, from both the Luther-Emery liquid and Luttinger-liquid states.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Metastable phase separation and information retrieval in multicomponent mixtures
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Liquid mixtures can separate into phases with distinct composition. This phenomenon has recently come back to prominence due to its role in complex biological liquids, such as the cytoplasm, which contain thousands of components. For simple two-component mixtures phase-separated states are global free energy minima. However, local free energy minima, i.e., metastable states, are known to play a dominant role in complex systems with many components. For example, Hopfield neural networks can retrieve stored information from partial cues via relaxation to metastable states. Under what conditions can phase separated states be metastable, and what are the implications for information retrieval in multicomponent liquids? In this work we develop the general thermodynamic formalism of metastable phase separation. We then apply this formalism to an illustrative toy example inspired by recent experiments, binary mixtures with high-order interactions. Finally, as core application of the formalism, we study metastability in Hopfield liquids, a class of multicomponent mixtures capable of storing information on the composition of phases. We show that these phases can be nucleated from partial cues via metastable phase separation. Spatial simulations of liquids with a large number of components match our analytical solution. Our work suggests that complex biological mixtures can retrieve information through metastable phase separation.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Gate-tunable Josephson parametric amplifiers based on semiconductor nanowires
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Superconductor-semiconductor hybrid materials have been extensively used for experiments on electrically tunable quantum devices. Notably, Josephson junctions utilizing nanowire weak links have enabled a number of new gate-tunable qubits, including gatemons, Andreev level qubits and spin qubits. Conversely, superconducting parametric amplifiers based on Josephson junctions have not yet been implemented using nanowires, even though such nearly quantum limited amplifiers are key elements in experiments on quantum circuits. Here we present Josephson parametric amplifiers based on arrays of parallel InAs nanowires that feature a large critical current as required for linear amplification. The resonance frequency of the devices is gate-tunable by almost 1 GHz, with a gain exceeding 20 dB in multiple frequencies and markedly improved noise performance compared to a low-temperature commercial amplifier. This platform enables on-chip integration of gate-tunable qubits with nearly quantum limited amplifiers using the same hybrid materials and on any substrate.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Ultra-transient grating spectroscopy for visualization of surface acoustics
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Ultrasonic wave propagation across material surfaces reveals essential information about the materials' elastic behavior. All direction- and frequency-dependent features of the propagation are encoded in the Green's function. Here we present a direct experimental visualization of the frequency-domain angle-resolved Green's function, including all its complexity resulting from elastic anisotropy. We achieve this visualization using transient grating spectroscopy (TGS), otherwise well established for measuring Rayleigh-type surface acoustic waves (SAWs). But here we focus on early-time thermoacoustic phenomena in the TGS experiment, revealing that, along with the transient standing-wave patterns of SAWs, there also emerge oscillations with at least an order of magnitude shorter lifetimes. These oscillations superpose into dynamic displacement patterns that are transient with respect to the classical transient timescales in TGS; the optical diffraction signal from these ultra-transient gratings enables capturing the surface acoustic response in full detail. By utilizing this feature, ultra-transient grating spectroscopy (UTGS) opens pathways for studying anisotropic materials.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Bond-resolved STM with density-based methods
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Bond-resolved scanning tunneling microscopy (BRSTM) provides intramolecular contrast with CO-functionalized tips, but its interpretation requires a description of both probe relaxation and orbital-dependent tunneling. We introduce a simulation framework that combines the Full-Density-Based Model (FDBM) for CO-tip relaxation with Chen's derivative rules applied directly to real-space density-functional-theory (DFT) wave functions. We test the method against a series of constant-height BRSTM images of perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhydride (PTCDA) on Ag(111), acquired in 10~pm tip-height increments, and published data for 1,5,9-trioxo-13-azatriangulene (TOAT) on Cu(111). The simulations reproduce the principal intramolecular contrast features and their evolution with tip height. The comparison identifies distinct roles for the substrate: it modifies the partially occupied molecular states and probe--sample forces in PTCDA/Ag(111), while its influence on the TOAT/Cu(111) contrast remains relevant even without substantial changes in molecular-orbital occupation. Our framework thus provides a practical and accurate route to interpreting BRSTM images that incorporates, from a single DFT calculation, the separate contributions of electronic structure and CO-tip relaxation.

arXiv_CondMat.title: The generic Mott transition in the sine-Gordon model through an embedded worm algorithm
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The generic Mott transition in one-dimensional quantum systems can be described by the sine-Gordon model with a tilt via bosonization. Because the configuration space of the sine-Gordon model separates into distinct topological sectors, standard local Monte Carlo schemes are limited to very small system sizes. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the smooth worm (SmoWo) Monte Carlo algorithm which enlarges the configuration space to allow smooth transitions between topological sectors. The method combines worm updates with event-chain Monte Carlo moves. We explicitly prove its validity and quantify its performance. Thanks to the substantial acceleration achieved by the SmoWo algorithm, we are able to simulate large system sizes, providing a precise picture of the different phases and critical behaviour of the sine-Gordon model.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Curvature Potential Formulation for Thin Elastic Sheets
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Thin sheets, from graphene to biological membranes, exhibit wrinkling, folding, and thermal deformations driven by geometric nonlinearities. They are treated using weakly nonlinear theories such as the F\"oppl-von K\'arm\'an equations, whose reliance on small slopes and a single-valued height field excludes large-slope and non-graph configurations even at small strain. We introduce a geometric reformulation in terms of scalar stress and curvature potentials that preserves the FvK structure while removing the graph restriction. We show that intrinsic symmetries of these potentials, as opposed to symmetries of the configuration, can persist when none is apparent in the embedding, enabling analytical solutions of boundary-value problems inaccessible to the conventional height-based formulation. Finite-element comparisons validate the predictions under strong confinement. Together, the extended validity and tractability open analytical routes to fluctuating membranes, ribbons, and architected sheets.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Thermodynamics of the $q$-deformed Kittel--Shore model
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The Kittel--Shore Hamiltonian characterizes $N$ spins with identical long-range interactions, and the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ coalgebra has been proven to be a symmetry of this model, which can be exactly solved. By using quantum groups and, in particular, $\mathfrak{su}_{q}(2)$, this Hamiltonian was deformed. In this work, we study the thermodynamic properties of this deformed model for spin-$1/2$ particles. In particular, we discuss how this deformation affects the specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, magnetisation, and phase transitions as a function of the parameter $q$ of the deformation and compare them with those of the undeformed model. Deformation was found to shift the thermodynamic behaviours to higher temperatures and alter the phase transitions. Additionally, we extend the framework to complex deformations on the unit circle, $q = e^{i\theta}$, for $q$ not being a root of unity. For an $N=4$ tetrahedral cluster, this phase establishes a thermodynamic equivalence between a second-neighbor spin-Hamiltonian and the $q$-deformed quantum model. At least, we have found experimental compounds well reproduced by the Kittel--Shore model for $N=4$. Validating our effective algebraic model against exact diagonalisation data for the $\text{Cu}_2\text{Te}_2\text{O}_5X_2$ ($X=\text{Cl}, \text{Br}$) compound family demonstrates that $\theta$ accurately reproduces the structural anisotropy.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Sound waves in a backreaction-affected analogue spacetime: acoustic metric, mass, and correlations in Bose-Einstein condensates
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Analogue gravity treats sound as a field on an effective spacetime set by the background flow, but quantum fluctuations feed back on this background. Whether a condensate modified by such backreaction still defines a spacetime for the quantum field remains open. Using a number-conserving expansion of a Bose-Einstein condensate, we show that in the sound-wave and eikonal approximations the first-order phase fluctuation propagates on an acoustic metric of the backreaction-corrected condensate and acquires a spacetime-dependent mass that cannot be absorbed into the metric. For a finite, quasi-one-dimensional gas after an interaction quench, backreaction enhances the equal-point phase correlation by about $10\%$ in the bulk and up to $20\%$ near the walls while the depletion remains below $2\%$; the bulk enhancement survives finite imaging resolution.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Controlling microalgae populations by phototactic memory
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Motile microorganisms navigate environments that vary in space and time by coupling sensory inputs to internal physiological states and active motion. In photosynthetic microorganisms, such coupling can be mediated by phototaxis, yet how temporal sensing combines with spatial variations of the environment to shape population organisation remains poorly understood. To probe this coupling, we expose populations of the phototactic microalga \textit{Chlamydomonas reinhardtii} to structured light landscapes. Under ring-shaped illumination, cells robustly accumulate at the center of the illuminated region, rather than at the light-intensity maximum. Single-cell tracking shows that cells steer relative to local intensity gradients and undergo a non-trivial phototactic response, where, on average, cells outside the ring perform positive phototaxis while cells inside perform negative phototaxis. Population experiments, numerical simulations and analytical modelling show that this trapping cannot be reproduced by an instantaneous switching rule, but requires a finite phototactic memory acting on the transition between positive and negative phototaxis. This internal timescale couples to the geometry of the light field and to the persistence of active motion, enabling controllable spatial localisation without physical confinement. Our results generically show how memory in a single-cell sensory response can control population-level organisation in a living active system.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Sparse Statistical Modeling in Condensed Matter Physics
arXiv_CondMat.summary: In this work we explore the possibility of using sparse statistical modeling in condensed matter physics. The procedure is employed to two well known problems: elemental superconductors and heavy fermions, and was shown that in most cases performs better than other AI methods, such as machine or deep learning. More importantly, sparse modeling has two major advantages over other methods: the ability to deal with small data sets and in particular its interpretabilty. Namely, sparse modeling can provide insight into the calculation process and allow the users to give physical interpretation of their results. We argue that many other problems in condensed matter physics would benefit from these properties of sparse statistical modeling.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Unifying Dirac Spin Liquids on Square and Shastry-Sutherland Lattices via Fermionic Deconfined Criticality
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We present a fermionic gauge theory for deconfined quantum criticality on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice and reveal its shared low-energy field-theoretic structure with the square lattice. Starting from an SU(2) $\pi$-flux parent state, we construct a continuum theory of Dirac spinons coupled to an SU(2) gauge field and adjoint Higgs fields whose condensates drive transitions to a staggered-flux U(1) spin liquid and a gapless $Z_{2}$ Dirac spin liquid. While the Shastry-Sutherland lattice permits additional symmetry-allowed fermion bilinears compared to the square lattice, the quantum field theories are identical up to additional irrelevant terms. Consequently, the Higgs potential structure and the leading low-energy theory coincide with the square-lattice case at the quantum critical point. The SO(5) critical point is expected to realize conformal deconfined criticality: we analyze it in a large-flavor expansion, calculate its critical exponents, and identify the Yukawa coupling between the fermions and Higgs fields as the relevant perturbation that destabilizes it, consistent with pseudocritical behavior observed in recent Monte Carlo studies. We show that the emergent SO(5) order parameter acquires a large anomalous dimension at the critical point, leading to strongly enhanced N\'eel and VBS susceptibilities-a hallmark of fermionic deconfined quantum criticality consistent with numerical studies. Our results place recent numerical evidence for a gapless $Z_{2}$ Dirac spin liquid on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice within a controlled field-theoretic framework and demonstrate that fermionic deconfined criticality on the square lattice-including critical exponents and stability-extends to frustrated lattices with reduced symmetry.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Deep-layered machines have a built-in Occam's razor
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Many complex systems map vast numbers of microscopic descriptions onto far fewer macroscopic outcomes. Surprisingly, these input-output maps strongly favor simple outputs. In an exactly solvable deep-layered machine, we prove that simplicity bias strengthens with every layer. The probability of an output function $F$ approaches $\Pr(F)\propto 2^{-K(F)}$, where $K$ is the Kolmogorov complexity. Our results show that hierarchical composition alone can generate an intrinsic Occam's razor, suggesting a general mechanism for simplicity bias in learning and evolution.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Kelvin-Helmholtz and counter-superflow instabilities driven by differential effective rotation in a three-component Bose-Einstein condensate
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Interfacial hydrodynamic instabilities in multicomponent superfluids provide a versatile platform to explore nonequilibrium quantum dynamics beyond classical fluid analogues. We study dynamical interfacial instabilities in a quasi-two-dimensional three-component Bose-Einstein condensate confined in a harmonic trap, where differential effective rotation between neighboring components is generated through selective phase imprinting. A component with an imprinted vorticity $l_j$ acquires an azimuthal phase winding $\phi_j = l_j\theta$, producing a superfluid velocity $v_\theta(r_j) = l_j\hbar/mr_j$ at interface radius $r_j$ and an effective angular velocity $\Omega_j^{\mathrm{eff}} = l_j\hbar/mr_j^2$. The differential effective rotation $\Delta\Omega_j^{\mathrm{eff}} = \Omega_j^{\mathrm{eff}} - \Omega_{j+1}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ between neighboring components constitutes the sole driver of interfacial shear and the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI). Three instability regimes are examined: KHI in the strongly immiscible limit, counter-superflow instability in the partially miscible regime, and a parameter window where both mechanisms coexist. A hydrodynamic pressure-balance model is derived, showing that the KHI onset condition depends only on $\Delta\Omega_j^{\mathrm{eff}}$. Time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii simulations and a Bogoliubov-de Gennes analysis identify the dominant unstable modes, whose spatial structures are consistent with the observed density modulations. The dominant azimuthal mode is set by a competition between shear-driven destabilization and surface-tension stabilization, confirmed by numerical simulations with different imprinted vorticities. The results show that a three-component condensate with two tunable interfaces provides a controlled platform for studying multicomponent quantum hydrodynamics, with instability dynamics significantly richer than those of binary mixtures.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Emergent thermal behavior, synchronization, and non-Hermitian phase transitions in driven-dissipative photon condensates
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Driven-dissipative Bose-Einstein condensates of photons in optical resonators have been shown theoretically to exist as a long-lived, yet metastable state stabilized by a ghost attractor, despite continuous driving [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 053402 (2025)]. Here we analyze the properties of this metastable condensate as well as the relaxation dynamics into and out of this state by means of the Lindblad master-equation approach, treating the condensate and the equal-time, noncondensed fluctuations on the same footing. Despite its nonequilibrium origin, the quasistationary condensate exhibits thermal behavior in that the order-parameter fluctuations scale with system size as in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the photon-number distribution in multimode resonators is in excellent agreement with a Bose-Einstein distribution. A linear stability analysis further reveals the presence of several exceptional points, resulting in multiple non-Hermitian phase transitions associated with the relaxation dynamics into and out of the metastable condensate. These behaviors reconcile apparently contradictory experimental results.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Scaling of Long-Range Loop-Erased Random Walks
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We study the scaling properties of long-range loop-erased random walks (LR-LERW), where the underlying random walker performs L\'evy-flight-like jumps with a power-law step-length distribution $P(\mathbf{r})\sim |\mathbf{r}|^{-(d+\sigma)}$. Using extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we measure the scaling relation $N \sim R^{d_N}$ between the loop-erased step number $N$ and the spatial extent $R$, and determine the geometric exponent $d_N$ for various values of $\sigma$ in spatial dimensions $d = 1, 2,$ and $3$, as well as at the marginal point $\sigma = 2$ in $d=4$ and $5$. We observe a continuous crossover from long-range (LR) to short-range (SR) behavior as $\sigma$ increases. Below the upper critical dimension $d< d/2$, loop erasure is asymptotically irrelevant and $d_N=\sigma$, consistent with L\'evy-flight scaling. For $d/2 < \sigma < 2$, loop erasure becomes relevant and $d_N$ varies continuously toward the SR-LERW value. At the marginal points with $\sigma=d/2$ or $\sigma=2$, clear logarithmic corrections are observed. At and above the upper critical dimension, $d \geq 4$, the scaling at $\sigma=2$ is found to be $N \sim R^2/\ln R$, consistent with that of the corresponding L\'evy flight. Our results provide a systematic numerical determination of $d_N(\sigma)$ for the LR-LERW across dimensions, and are consistent with $\sigma_* = 2$ as the boundary between LR and SR critical behaviors recently established in a broad variety of statistical models.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Chiral vortical effect and boundary-induced vortical pumping in finite Weyl systems
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The chiral vortical effect (CVE) -- an axial current driven by rotation in chiral matter -- appears in systems ranging from relativistic fluids to Weyl semimetals. We present a quantum treatment of a rotating Weyl fermion in a finite cylinder that reproduces the on-axis current density obtained by Vilenkin in an infinite system, while revealing two new phenomena. First, we find that the cross-sectional averaged current density vanishes in the thermodynamic limit, establishing that the bulk vortical response is purely a magnetization current. Second, for spin-polarized boundary conditions, we uncover a robust family of chiral modes that transport axial charge, $\Delta Q=\chi N^2\Delta\theta/4\pi$, under rotation by angle $\Delta\theta$, where $\chi$ is the Weyl node chirality and $N$ is the number of chiral modes. The pump is independent of temperature, Fermi level, and Weyl velocities, but depends on the UV-sensitive number $N$. These results clarify the quantum structure of the bulk CVE and reveal a boundary-enforced chiral spectral structure underlying vortical response in Weyl systems.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Conductivity of charge-neutral multicomponent 2D electron-hole system
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The interplay between distinct carrier species in systems with broken Galilean invariance can give rise to a rich landscape of interaction-driven transport phenomena. Here, we develop a comprehensive theory of the electrical conductivity of a two-dimensional mixture of massless Dirac and massive fermions, a system realized in HgTe quantum wells tuned to the charge-neutrality point. In this regime, all carriers are thermally activated, enabling a self-consistent, temperature-dependent interplay between the two species. Crucially, the charge-neutrality condition ensures that the chemical potential is not externally pinned but is determined self-consistently, thereby making the system's transport response an intrinsic probe of inter-species quantum friction. We demonstrate that the conductivity changes with temperature : at low temperatures, transport is dominated by massless Dirac carriers, yielding a nearly temperature-independent conductivity reminiscent of the charge-neutrality point in pristine graphene. As the temperature rises, massive holes become thermally excited, and their mutual scattering with Dirac carriers induces a specific nonmonotonic temperature dependence of the conductivity in both clean and disordered structures. In particular, in nearly clean structures with strong screening modeled by a short-range interparticle interaction potential, the system's conductivity can exhibit an inverse-quadratic temperature dependence. Conversely, in disordered structures with a long-range interparticle interaction, it varies quadratically with temperature. Our findings establish HgTe quantum wells at charge neutrality as a clean, highly tunable platform for isolating and quantitatively studying interaction-driven transport in the absence of Galilean invariance, offering a direct pathway to explore regimes where interparticle collisions dominate over disorder.
authors: V. M. Kovalev, I. G. Savenko

arXiv_CondMat.title: Pressure-Driven Activation of Semi-core p-Orbitals in Rb and Cs via Crystal-Field Splitting
arXiv_CondMat.summary: High-pressure unconventional oxidation states are attributed to exceptional charge transfer, which is itself induced by the differential pressure response of atomic orbital energy levels. The high oxidation states observed in heavy alkali metals (Cs, Ba, Ra) exemplify this behavior, as their semi-core p-states surpass the valence orbital levels of oxidants, e.g., the 2p-orbital of F, at high pressure. However, semi-core p-electron activation in lighter alkali metals, such as Rb, is hindered because the relative orbitals lie at intrinsically lower energies due to their smaller radii, making pressure-induced upshift challenging. We demonstrate that crystal-field splitting of alkali-metal semi-core p-orbitals selectively elevates a portion of these states, substantially lowering the pressure threshold for their chemical activation. Here, our computations reveal that the semi-core 4p-electrons of Rb form weak metallic bonds with F in $P2_1/c$-RbBF5 at around 250 GPa, a pressure accessible in modern high-pressure experiments. Extending to Cs-B-F systems, the crystal-field splitting drives 5p participation in Cs-F bond formation in CsBF5. These findings unveil a new paradigm for semi-core or inner-shell chemistry, providing a unifying framework for semi-core electron activation and bonding. Crucially, they establish that semi-core electrons of light main-group elements, including Rb, are accessible at experimentally feasible pressures.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Singlet-only always-on gapless exchange (SAGE) spin qubits: Charge noise effects and two-qubit gates
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Singlet-only always-on gapless exchange (SAGE) spin qubits are an alternative type of exchange-only (EO) qubits that encode a single qubit in the spins of four electrons located in four tunnel-coupled quantum dots. While conventional EO qubits are susceptible to local magnetic field gradients caused by local nuclear environments and $g$-factor variations, the SAGE qubit subspace is inherently protected from magnetic-gradient-induced Pauli errors by virtue of the singlet-only encoding, which is invariant under magnetic field gradients, and the always-on exchange couplings, which provide energetic leakage protection. However, the always-on operation simultaneously increases the qubit's sensitivity to charge noise. Here, starting from a Hubbard model describing the underlying electronic structure of the coupled quantum dots, we characterize the performance of SAGE qubits in the presence of $1/f$ charge noise that induces fluctuations in both the dot chemical potentials and the interdot tunnel couplings. We calculate SAGE idle coherence times and show that realistic CPMG-like pulse sequences can be used to significantly extend SAGE single-qubit coherence times for experimentally relevant charge noise strengths. We likewise study the fidelity of SAGE two-qubit gates in the presence of charge and magnetic noise and again propose a simple refocusing strategy to mitigate the noise, while increased ramp times of the entangling pulse suppress leakage into noncomputational states.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Ground state of the Hubbard model with spin-dependent linear potential
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigate the competition between attractive spin-spin interactions and spin-separating external forces in the ground state of a one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. We consider a lattice with open boundary conditions, subject to a linear external potential whose gradient is opposite for the two spin components, so that each spin species sees a potential minimum at a different end of the lattice. Using density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) simulations, we map the ground-state density distributions and the number of doubly occupied sites as a function of the potential gradient $\beta$ and interaction strength. We identify three distinct regimes separated by critical threshold gradients: (i) a small-$\beta$ regime where fermion pairing remains robust against the external potential; (ii) an intermediate-$\beta$ phase-separated regime characterized by a staircase-like decrease in the doublon number, corresponding to the successive, one-by-one breaking of bound pairs; and (iii) a large-$\beta$ regime where the two spin components are completely spatially separated. We complement the numerical results with a phenomenological model and a local-density approximation analysis, from which we derive closed-form analytical estimates for these critical threshold values. We also verify that the staircase structure persists under additional harmonic confinement. Our results are directly testable in cold-atom experiments, and demonstrate that a spin-dependent linear potential enables precise, integer-level control of the number of bound fermion pairs.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Thermal bottleneck in a freely suspended superconducting island on InAs nanowire
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigate the heat balance in superconducting islands (S-islands) formed in epitaxial Al/InAs nanowires (NWs) freely suspended above the substrate. We employ a Joule spectroscopy approach, which traces the superconductor-normal transition in the S-island mediated by heating of the neighboring InAs NW segments via transport current. The temperature of the surrounding 3He bath is varied with nearby mesoscopic heaters and controlled with the NW Johnson noise thermometry. The experiment reveals a substantial thermal relaxation bottleneck associated with the cooling via surrounding 3He, which gives rise to phonon heating in the S-island. Our results uncover the role of environmental cooling in non-equilibrium experiments in S-islands in NW devices.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Anomalous thermal and elastic properties of an epitaxial NiTi film exhibiting R-phase
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Shape memory alloys like NiTi are at the core of emerging thermal management applications, including elastocaloric refrigeration, thermoelastic harvesting, and latent heat storage. Most of these applications benefit from a small scale due to the accelerated heat exchange, but obtaining precise functional properties of films is challenging. Here we demonstrate that transient grating spectroscopy (TGS) enables characterization of elastic coefficients and thermal diffusivity of a 3 $\mu$m thick epitaxial NiTi film during a thermally induced phase transformation. The in-situ measurement of a complete austenite$\rightarrow$R-phase$\rightarrow$martensite$\rightarrow$austenite temperature cycle reveals that the elastic properties exhibit a crossover of the shear moduli (from $c^\prime < c_{44}$ in austenite to $c^\prime > c_{44}$ in martensite) and that the thermal diffusivity changes by a factor of {4.5} between the R-phase and austenite. This dramatic change, together with the absence of hysteresis between the R-phase and austenite, makes NiTi a promising material candidate for thermal switches. The results indicate that the change in thermal diffusivity originates from an anomalous heat capacity of the R-phase. Furthermore, our TGS study provides temperature-dependent thermal and elastic properties required for simulating thermal management microsystems using this material.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Dynamic Eikonal Attenuation and Mutual Coherence of Quantum Particles due to Equilibrium Coulomb Fluctuations
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We develop a dynamic theory of eikonal attenuation and mutual coherence for a quantum particle propagating through equilibrium Coulomb fluctuations. The one-particle length $\ell$ is the attenuation length of the ensemble-averaged retarded propagator, not an Anderson localization length or a transport mean free path. For a collisionless classical one-component plasma (OCP), the potential spectrum follows from the fluctuation--dissipation theorem and the RPA dielectric function. In suitable plasma parameter windows, both fast and slow probe regimes are physically meaningful. Fast probes recover the Coulomb logarithm with the dynamical infrared length $v/\omega_{\rm p}$. Slow probes yield $G(v)\propto v$ and, in the controlled weak branch, $\ell\propto k$. We derive an exact finite-thickness mutual-coherence expression and a closed slow-regime transverse scaling function. Within the controlled slow-OCP and thick-slab window, the logarithmic two-ray visibility scales as $v^{-1}$ at fixed transverse separation, in contrast to the $v^{-2}$ dependence for frozen finite-slab fluctuations. For a symmetric diffusive electrolyte, linearized stochastic density functional theory gives the exact on-shell result $G_{\rm el}(v)=(m^2C/\hbar^4)\operatorname{arsinh}[v/(2D\kappa)]$, where $C=k_{\mathrm B}Tq_0^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_b)$. For ordinary liquid electrolytes, the slow diffusive limit is inaccessible within the spatial eikonal regime and is therefore a formal asymptote. The physically relevant electrolyte limit is instead that of a fast probe, $v\gg D\kappa$, where the diffusive charge relaxation generates an intrinsic infrared length $v/(D\kappa^2)$ absent from the quasi-static theory.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Planckian dissipation from classical hydrodynamics
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Hydrodynamics describes the long-time, long-distance dynamics of interacting quantum systems by classical equations, yet at low temperature quantum fluctuations might eventually invalidate this classical picture. Here we ask what it takes for a quantum system to sustain a consistently classical hydrodynamic description. Our starting point is the quantum fluctuation-dissipation theorem which, when read in the time domain, acts as a blurring of the fine details of correlation functions on a Planckian time-scale. We analyse how this blurring interacts with the diffusive large-deviation form of correlators assuming the existence of a hydrodynamic light cone velocity, and show that the interior of the cone splits into a classical region, where correlation and response satisfy the classical fluctuation-dissipation relation, and a quantum region, where they deviate sharply from it. We illustrate the mechanism on three phenomenological hydrodynamic equations - diffusion, telegraph and diffusive-telegraph. Preserving a finite classical region as the temperature is lowered forces the current relaxation rate to be bounded from above by the Planckian rate. This bound connects to bounds on diffusivity, equilibration time and shear viscosity. In this way, a Planckian bound on dissipation emerges not as a quantum constraint on microscopic dynamics, but as the price a system pays to remain describable by classical hydrodynamics down to low temperatures.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Topological metal-insulator transitions in one-dimensional non-Hermitian quasicrystals: beyond PT-symmetry
arXiv_CondMat.summary: One-dimensional non-Hermitian quasicrystals with parity and time-reversal (PT) symmetry can simultaneously exhibit localization-delocalization transition, topological phase transition, and PT-symmetry-breaking transition. This motivates us to investigate how the absence of PT symmetry impacts topological metal-insulator transitions in non-Hermitian quasicrystals. We propose a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic model that generally does not preserve PT-symmetry but, in most parameter regions, hosts a generic triple-transition scenario encompassing localization, topological, and degeneracy-breaking transitions. These transitions can be understood within the dual momentum-space representation featuring asymmetric couplings. Specifically, the localization boundary is obtained from the dual momentum-space representation by comparing the Lyapunov exponent, or inverse localization length, of the reciprocal Aubry-Andr\'e model with the nonreciprocal hopping-asymmetry ratio of the dual lattice. The accompanying topological transition is characterized by a point-gap winding number defined with respect to a reference energy inside the complex spectral gap, whereas the degeneracy-breaking transition is understood from the loss of the reciprocal $n\leftrightarrow -n$ spectral symmetry. The system also exhibits a localization-delocalization transition analogous to that in the Hermitian case, which occurs without accompanying topological or degeneracy-breaking transitions. Our work extends the topological metal-insulator transitions previously studied in PT-symmetric systems to a more general class of non-Hermitian setting, and further reveals that non-Hermitian systems can host distinct types of localization behavior.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Reflective Metastructure Q-plate for Ultrashort Laser Pulses
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The orbital angular momentum of light is an intriguing property for developing light driven applications. It emerged as an independent degree of freedom by which to manipulate light and, consequently, the interaction of light with matter. Several methods exist for the generation of light carrying orbital angular momentum, mostly employing transmitting or reflecting optical components, which radially modulate the phase profile of the light. As one of such components, transmissive q-plates established themselves as standard elements due to their usability over a broad wavelength range. Here, we present our approach to building a highly reflective q-plate with a diameter of 4.5 mm based on a plasmonic metasurface capable of converting orbital angular momentum from the nanostructure to ultrashort laser pulses without measurable temporal broadening under the investigated conditions. We highlight its working principle over a wide range of wavelengths for reflection under normal and grazing incidence.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Overview of the Theory of Extremely Correlated Fermi Liquids
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The Extremely Correlated Fermi Liquids (ECFL) theory is reviewed as a framework for understanding the $t$-$J$ model in metallic systems close to the Mott insulating limit. This overview presents the underlying ideas and the resulting equations in a form accessible to nonexperts. We compare theoretical results with all available resistivity data for single-layer High-T$_{c}$ systems, and with some spectral data. The highlighted results include a density dependent quasilinear T-dependence in resistivity, an unusually small quasiparticle weight, and distinct low-temperature emergent scales that dominate transport, thermodynamics and spectral properties of single-layer High T$_c$ systems. Suggestions are made for further experiments to probe the physics of these challenging quantum many-body systems.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Coexistence of Donor and Acceptor Hydrogen States in n-Type InN
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Hydrogen often exhibits amphoteric behavior in semiconductors, but its role is in n-type InN remains unresolved. Wurtzite InN is a narrow-gap semiconductor with high electron mobility and is therefore attractive for high-speed electronics and optoelectronic applications. Here we use hard x-ray photoemission spectroscopy (HAXPES) to probe hydrogen-related electronic structure in as-grown and post-annealed InN thin films prepared at different grown temperatures. Post annealing, which reduces the concentration of hydrogen impurities in the films, shifts the core-level spectra toward lower binding energy, consistent with a chemical-potential shift associated with the passivation of electron carriers. In the valence-band spectra, an acceptor-like in-gap feature near the valence-band maximum is suppressed after annealing. Together with the established donor-like behavior of hydrogen in InN, these results suggest that acceptor H- states coexist with donor H+ states in InN. The coexistence of these opposite hydrogen charge states provides a microscopic picture of hydrogen-driven compensation in InN and highlights the amphoteric nature of hydrogen even in a highly n-type semiconductor.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Generalized Fourier's law in mesoscopic systems
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Fourier's law fails when the mean free path of the energy carriers becomes comparable to the length and time scales over which the temperature field varies. We derive a thermodynamically consistent generalization in which the conductivity becomes a nonlocal memory operator $\mathbf{\kappa}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{k},\omega)$, by combining mesoscopic nonequilibrium thermodynamics with the Mori--Kubo--Zwanzig projection-operator formalism. The Onsager kernel is a tensor sum over vibrational normal modes weighted by their Bose heat capacities and relaxation functions; it satisfies the second law for any closure consistent with the fluctuation--dissipation theorem and reduces, in the relaxation-time closure, to the nonlocal conductivity of the phonon Boltzmann equation. Two consequences follow. First, direction-dependent sampling of this tensor in a pump--probe experiment makes a nominally isotropic crystal exhibit apparent conductivities $\Lambda_z\neq\Lambda_r$. Second, the modulation frequency does not introduce temporal memory but sets the probed wavevector through the thermal penetration depth, so that the frequency-dependent suppression of the apparent conductivity measured by time-domain thermoreflectance on Ge and SiGe alloys is a spatial-nonlocality effect, with effective lengths of $0.25$--$0.4~\mu$m. With published mean-free-path spectra and no parameter adjusted to the thermoreflectance data, the kernel reproduces the spot-size dependence of Si, the frequency dependence of the apparent conductivity of Ge and Si$_{0.2}$Ge$_{0.8}$ and the rise of the apparent interface conductance of Al/Si$_{0.99}$Ge$_{0.01}$, and contains the two-channel ballistic/diffusive model as a two-sector projection.
authors: Luciano C. Lapas (Latin American Institute of Life

arXiv_CondMat.title: Specific absorption rate of uniaxial single-domain nanomagnets: stochastic spin dynamics versus linear response theory
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We compute the specific absorption rate of a uniaxial single-domain nanomagnet driven by an alternating magnetic field by two methods: i) direct numerical integration of the stochastic (Langevin) Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert equation (the LLL approach), and ii) linear response theory (LRT) based on the Debye susceptibility with the N\'eel relaxation time $\ta$. We first analytically show that both methods are equivalent for small magnetic field amplitude, and then compute their deviation $\Lambda\equiv\SAR_{\LLL}/\SAR_{\LRT}-1$ as a function of the magnetic field amplitude for two temperatures chosen on opposite sides of the Debye resonance. One of the main results is that the sign and magnitude of $\Lambda$ are governed by the dimensionless product $\om\ta$, in addition to the linearity parameter $\xi=\mu_{s}B_{0}/k_{B}T$ for the easy-axis geometry considered here. Indeed, below resonance ($\om\ta<1$), linear response theory overestimates the specific absorption rate, whereas above resonance ($\om\ta>1$, the regime typical of blocked nanoparticles) linear response theory can underestimate the specific absorption rate by up to $\sim70\%$ at $\xi\sim2$. We expect this work to provide a quantitative guidance for the use of linear response theory in magnetic hyperthermia and related nanoscale heat-transport problems, and to serve as a single-particle benchmark for extensions to many-spin and interacting systems.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Monte Carlo solution of the Kondo model
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The Kondo model is a paradigmatic quantum impurity problem realized in a wide variety of experimental platforms and central to the study of strongly correlated electrons. We introduce a discrete model that exactly reproduces the multichannel Kondo model and demonstrate that it can be simulated efficiently. Using cluster Monte Carlo algorithms, we completely eliminate critical slowing down, providing direct access to universal crossover functions and transport properties across a broad range of parameters. Remarkably, the same model captures both the weak- and strong-coupling regimes, unifying descriptions traditionally derived in complementary limits and revealing their common origin. Our method naturally accommodates large channel numbers, anisotropy, interacting one-dimensional leads, and channel asymmetry, yielding predictions for transport properties in charge-Kondo devices.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Decoupling Strain-Rate Sensitivity and Deformation Length Scale Effects in Neutron-Irradiated Tungsten: A Coupled Nano-Indentation, HR-EBSD and Crystal Plasticity Study
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Strain-rate-dependent deformation in spherical nanoindentation couples material rate sensitivity effects with the evolving contact radius, penetration depth and plastic-zone size. A rate-sensitive model where loading rate and indentation depth are prescribed independently allows their contributions to be disentangled. We study this in unirradiated and neutron-irradiated single-crystal tungsten, indented to the same final indentation strain at nominal strain-rates of 3.2e-5 to 3.2e-3 per second and reaching different final depths. Surface pile-up, residual lattice strain and dislocation distributions were measured by AFM and HR-EBSD. A rate-sensitive, strain-gradient crystal plasticity framework, incorporating thermally activated slip and irradiation hardening derived from measured defect populations, was calibrated at the highest strain rate and reproduced all these observables at the two lower strain rates without further parameter adjustment. The framework was then used to vary strain rate and depth independently. At fixed depth, strain rate over the experimental range changes the predicted peak load by < 1% and the pile-up by < 2 nm. At fixed strain rate, the experimental depth differences alone produce pile-up increases of ~ 90% and 130%, comparable to the measured 66% and 150% for unirradiated and irradiated tungsten. The measured differences between strain rate conditions therefore predominantly reflect the different depths reached; a 10% difference in final depth mimics more than an order of magnitude change in strain rate. Irradiation is seen to promote localisation, with its effect on pile-up increasing with depth up to ~ 500 nm, while remaining consistent with a common thermally activated deformation mechanism.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Inference Limits of Routine Cement Characterization for CEM I Performance: Evidence From a Multi-Producer Dataset
arXiv_CondMat.summary: This study evaluates the prediction of 28-day compressive strength from routine cement characterization across independent producers. Industrial records from 23 European producers cover nearly three decades of testing in a single laboratory, encompassing 476 samples. The archive includes CEM I, CEM II, CEM III, and other blended cements, with the main analysis focused on CEM I. Chemistry and fineness descriptors were evaluated using linear and nonlinear models. Strength class and water demand were also examined as performance labels from standardized testing. Mean absolute errors in 28-day strength prediction were approximately 3 MPa, with linear models performing comparably to nonlinear models. Producer holdout tests assessed transfer to cements from producers excluded from training and yielded absolute errors of the same order. Equivalent alkali showed a consistent negative association with 28-day strength, with K$_2$O carrying most of this signal. Together, these results highlight the value of industrial data collected under common laboratory conditions for interpretable 28-day strength prediction, with potential to inform cement design targeting lower production costs and CO$_2$ emissions.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Dimensional crossover in ultradilute Bose-Bose liquid mixtures
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We study ultradilute $^{39}$K Bose-Bose bulk mixtures and droplets in an external harmonic potential that confines them in one spatial direction towards the two-dimensional (2D) limit. Equations of state for several confinements are obtained with quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) at $T=0$, using interaction potentials that include information on the $s$-wave scattering length $a$ and the effective range $r_{\rm eff}$. Performing the calculations using two different interaction potential models we have determined the range of confinements for which equations of state are universal in terms of $a$ and $r_{\rm eff}$. Based on the QMC equation of state, we develop a 2D QMC density functional for each confinement strength and use it together with the local density approximation to determine properties of the self-bound drops. For moderate squeezing, energies and droplet profiles obtained using the 2D QMC functional agree well with those obtained using 3D functionals, while offering a substantial reduction in computational cost, and a consistent approach in crossover to 2D. Noticeably, our results approach 2D mean-field (MF) + Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) predictions only for the most strongly confined systems for which universality in terms of $a$ and $r_{\rm eff}$ is observed. This implies a very narrow range of confinements for which 2D LHY functionals are applicable, which affects the study of vortices using 2D functionals.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Updated Tkatchenko Scheffler method and assessment of dispersion methods for alkali-containing systems
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The Tkatchenko-Scheffler (TS) pairwise method to calculate dispersion interactions is a widely used approach to incorporate missing long-range van der Waals contributions in semilocal and hybrid density functional calculations. Despite subsequent many-body extensions, this formulation remains widely used. In 2018, Fedorov et al. reported updated van der Waals radii to the seminal work published in 2009. The present work examines the accuracy of the TS method with updated van der Waals radii (TS_2018), coupled with the semilocal Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional, for structural predictions of semiconducting and insulating materials. Special attention is paid to materials containing alkali elements, for which the TS_2009 method exhibits a large overbinding, associated with potentially large errors in predicted atomic structures. We also consider a narrower reformulation (TS_alkali) where only the the alkali atoms are corrected, so the method remains otherwise compatible with TS_2009. We compare these methods with a broader set of dispersion corrections--the DFT-D3 method, the exchange-hole dipole moment method, and the beyond-pairwise, nonlocal many-body dispersion method--for ionic and alkali-containing systems more generally. We examine equilibrium geometry predictions for 45 inorganic solid compounds as well as three Cs-containing halide perovskites, CsPb$X_3$ ($X$ = Cl, Br, I). Our results show that the updated van der Waals radii in the TS_2018 and TS_alkali methods resolve the overbinding that is present with TS_2009 in alkali-containing systems, bringing predictions into closer agreement with other dispersion methods. For the halide perovskites, method-dependent differences in predicted cell volumes and shapes persist, and no approach performs with perfect accuracy on all metrics for all three materials.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Spin-Chirality-Driven Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in van der Waals Magnet CrSBr
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) manifests with remarkable diversity in magnetic materials. Here, we establish vector spin chirality as a tunable knob for generating an unconventional time-reversal-even magnetic BPVE, comprising the chiral shift current (CSC) and chiral injection current (CIC). Using bilayer antiferromagnetic (AFM) CrSBr as a prototype, we theoretically demonstrate the emergence of CSC and CIC. Compared with conventional photovoltaic currents arising from noncentrosymmetric crystal structures or collinear magnetic orderings, CSC and CIC not only possess comparable magnitudes but also exhibit exceptional tunability. Specifically, they can be switched on and off by magnetic-field-induced spin canting, reversed in direction upon canting-direction reversal, and continuously modulated in intensity via canting-angle variation. Furthermore, we reveal an unusual optical transition channel governing both currents in CrSBr. Our work establishes an unconventional magnetic BPVE with remarkable controllability, offering opportunities for optoelectronic and magnetic-sensing applications in noncollinear magnets.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Transport-Noise and Optical Witnesses of Electronic Multipartite Entanglement
